storylines.label: NVIDIA Nemotron
storylines.latest_title: NVIDIA Nemotron 3.5 Super VL is now available in Amazon SageMaker JumpStart

editorial.tldr: NVIDIA's open Nemotron family widened on Oct 28 with Nemotron 3.5 Transcribe and Granary v2 for promptable multilingual transcription. A day later AWS published a guide to running the 120B-parameter Nemotron 3.5 Super VL on Amazon EKS and SageMaker HyperPod EKS.
editorial.whats_new: Nemotron 3.5 Super VL, a 120B-parameter multimodal model, is now a managed option in Amazon SageMaker JumpStart, deployable as an NVFP4 or BF16 variant.
editorial.why_it_matters: Nemotron 3.5 now has two AWS deployment paths, self-managed Kubernetes (EKS, HyperPod EKS) and managed JumpStart, plus a speech model, so an open-weight stack can be trialed without building serving infrastructure first.
editorial.take_for_builders: If you run multimodal agents on AWS, deploy both the NVFP4 and BF16 Super VL variants from JumpStart against your own eval set and compare cost and accuracy before choosing one.

status.detail: Nemotron 3.5 has moved from model releases to packaged deployment on AWS, with Super VL now in JumpStart.

storylines.label: Control Plane
storylines.latest_title: Introducing Control Room: Human control over AI workloads

editorial.tldr: Late October brought three Show HN projects pitching a control room or control plane for LLM agents: God, flightdeck, and Omneum. On Nov 4 the vLLM blog introduced Kinference, an open source inference control plane for vLLM on Kubernetes.
editorial.whats_new: OpenAI published two Control Room posts on Nov 9: a central system that tracks model workloads across its research infrastructure and can rapidly stop them when safety or security concerns arise.
editorial.why_it_matters: The label now spans three layers: agent observability, inference serving, and kill-switch control over training and research workloads. Check which layer a "control plane" actually governs before adopting it.
editorial.take_for_builders: If you run vLLM on Kubernetes, evaluate Kinference for per-tenant rate limits and cost tracking in a staging cluster. Treat the Show HN agent tools as early experiments and OpenAI's Control Room as a design reference, not something you can deploy.

status.detail: Independent projects keep using "control plane" or "control room" for different layers; OpenAI's Control Room is the latest and an internal system, not a product.

storylines.label: Long-Term Memory
storylines.latest_title: Show HN: MemSeal – provenance containment for agent long-term memory

editorial.tldr: Agent-memory research started with structured retrieval: ActionRAG (Oct 23) used graph diffusion for relation-consistent evidence, and ETAMem (Oct 27) separated and aligned heterogeneous memory types. Early November papers turned to consistency, task-conditioned utility and exploration-task benchmarks.
editorial.whats_new: A Nov 9 Show HN project, MemSeal, pitches provenance containment for agent long-term memory, a trust angle the research papers in this thread had not yet covered.
editorial.why_it_matters: Memory work now spans retrieval, consistency, utility and, with MemSeal, provenance: where a stored memory came from and what it may influence. A production memory layer needs tests for each, and the new item is a project announcement, not a reviewed result.
editorial.take_for_builders: Replay your own long-running agent traces against a plain retrieval baseline, test that changing an upstream fact updates dependent memories, and record where each memory came from; treat the papers as unreplicated preprints and MemSeal as unevaluated until it publishes results.

status.detail: Work has moved from retrieval design to consistency, utility and benchmarks, and now a provenance-focused open-source project; the research items are unreplicated arXiv preprints.

storylines.label: Claude Opus
storylines.latest_title: Which Claude model should you build with? Fable, Opus, Sonnet, or Haiku

editorial.tldr: Claude Opus 5.5 and Sonnet 5.5 reached Google Antigravity on Oct 20, giving developers a per-task model choice inside an agentic IDE. Three days later R&D World set Moonshot's Kimi K3.1 Pro against Opus 5.5 and GPT-6 Astra, making Opus 5.5 the reference point for open-weight challengers.
editorial.whats_new: Anthropic's Nov 9 guide compares Fable, Opus, Sonnet and Haiku on cost and use, and shows how to combine them, so model routing is now documented first-party guidance.
editorial.why_it_matters: Opus 5.5 is both the model teams route to and the yardstick Kimi K3.1 Pro is measured against, so tiering and challenger evals now rest on the same baseline.
editorial.take_for_builders: Read Anthropic's Nov 9 tiering guide against your current routing, and rerun your own evals on Opus 5.5 versus Kimi K3.1 Pro before moving any traffic, since the comparison item reports no verified results.

status.detail: The thread now spans Opus 5.5 distribution, a Kimi K3.1 Pro comparison against it, and Anthropic's own model-selection guidance; the items here do not report independent eval results.

storylines.label: Inference Kubernetes
storylines.latest_title: Podcast: Distributed LLM Inference on Kubernetes with llm-d, Wasm, & TornadoVM

editorial.tldr: On Nov 4 the vLLM project introduced Kinference, an open source inference control plane for vLLM on Kubernetes. A benchmark post comparing it against plain Kubernetes followed a day later.
editorial.whats_new: An InfoQ podcast (Nov 9) places llm-d and vLLM on Kubernetes in the wider distributed-inference conversation, alongside WebAssembly on the backend and TornadoVM for Java on GPUs.
editorial.why_it_matters: Serving LLMs on Kubernetes is moving from generic pod scheduling toward inference-aware control planes (token rate limiting, tenant cost tracking, load balancing), which changes what a platform team builds versus adopts.
editorial.take_for_builders: If you run vLLM on Kubernetes, read the Kinference benchmark methodology and rerun it on your own traffic mix before replacing your current routing and rate limiting.

status.detail: Inference-aware Kubernetes tooling is getting launch, benchmark and practitioner coverage, but only one benchmark post exists so far.

storylines.label: DeepSeek Open-sources
storylines.latest_title: VindexLLM – Windows Vulkan GPU GGUF LLM inference engine written in Delphi 12

editorial.tldr: DeepSeek open-sourced DeepInfer, the inference engine behind its production services, on Oct 20. On Oct 31 it published the architecture of an always-on coding agent, dsh-superagent.
editorial.whats_new: Coverage of the dsh-superagent prototype, a router-worker coding agent that watches team chat for work, continued through Nov 4, while the rest of the thread is third-party inference-engine news.
editorial.why_it_matters: DeepSeek is releasing both the serving layer (DeepInfer, reportedly 155T tokens/day) and an agent harness, so platform teams can inspect a production-scale stack, but the cost and throughput figures come from DeepSeek and press reports, not independent benchmarks.
editorial.take_for_builders: Before adopting DeepInfer or dsh-superagent, check license terms and hardware support, and benchmark them against your current serving stack rather than relying on the quoted token-per-day numbers.

status.detail: Two DeepSeek open-source drops, DeepInfer and dsh-superagent, with no independent benchmarks yet.

storylines.label: Kimi K3.1
storylines.latest_title: Huawei Ascend Adapts Kimi K3.1 Pro for LoRA Fine-Tuning on a 128-Card Atlas 950 SuperPoD

editorial.tldr: Moonshot AI's Kimi K3.1 Pro surfaced after Arena testing on Oct 23 and launched Oct 24 as a multi-trillion-parameter flagship served via API. A botched launch forced a quota reset and apology, and third-party hosts started listing it within days.
editorial.whats_new: Huawei Ascend now supports LoRA fine-tuning of Kimi K3.1 Pro on a 128-card Atlas 950 SuperPoD, following Moore Threads day-zero serving support and the Nov 5 open-weights release.
editorial.why_it_matters: Open weights plus day-0 vLLM and non-NVIDIA accelerator support make Kimi K3.1 Pro a self-hostable and fine-tunable frontier-class option, though at roughly 1.56TB of weights it is a large-cluster deployment.
editorial.take_for_builders: Read the weights license commercial-use conditions before planning self-hosting, budget for a large multi-GPU cluster given the 1.56TB checkpoint, and keep a fallback model since the hosted API had quota problems at launch.

status.detail: Weights are public with conditional commercial use, and inference and fine-tuning support is spreading across engines, clouds and domestic Chinese accelerators.

storylines.label: Retrieval-Augmented Generation
storylines.latest_title: Compaction, decay and reinforcement in a two-tier conversational memory: a paired evaluation against retrieval-augmented generation

editorial.tldr: Late-October research targeted the retriever: a paper trained embedding models on their own mistakes so multi-hop questions find all the evidence they need. A November 2 paper, TRIO, then argued that current RAG approaches are still far from satisfactory.
editorial.whats_new: A Nov 6 paper compares RAG over a raw transcript against a two-tier memory that compacts each turn into atomic facts, testing whether conversational agents should keep the transcript at all.
editorial.why_it_matters: RAG design choices (what you index, how the retriever is trained, what an agent remembers) are now being tested against alternatives, so the default pipeline is no longer a safe assumption.
editorial.take_for_builders: If you run conversational memory over a raw transcript, rerun your own recall evals against a compacted-facts variant before changing anything; treat these papers as hypotheses until reproduced on your data.

status.detail: Three arXiv papers in nine days probe different RAG layers: retriever training, task refinement, and agent memory.

storylines.label: Large Language
storylines.latest_title: ROSE: Risk-Aware Orthogonal Subspace Navigation for Lifelong Knowledge Editing in Multimodal Large Language Models

editorial.tldr: This thread is a broad reading list on LLM behavior, reliability and knowledge rather than one event. Oct 20-28 papers covered hallucination, steering and evals, then Mistral Large 4 landed on Hugging Face and vLLM on Oct 29 as work shifted to memory and retrieval.
editorial.whats_new: Nov 6: the ROSE preprint proposes risk-aware subspace navigation for lifelong knowledge editing in multimodal LLMs, targeting locality erosion and catastrophic forgetting when facts are updated.
editorial.why_it_matters: The practical thread is knowledge handling: retrieval, memory, editing and context trimming decide agent reliability and token spend more than any single model release here.
editorial.take_for_builders: If agent token limits bite, measure context trimming and caching against your own eval set before adopting it; treat the preprints and the Show HN tool as unreplicated.

storylines.label: Reasoning Multimodal
storylines.latest_title: ROSE: Risk-Aware Orthogonal Subspace Navigation for Lifelong Knowledge Editing in Multimodal Large Language Models

editorial.tldr: Late-October papers focused on getting reasoning into multimodal models: reasoning-augmented embeddings, latent communication between vision and small language models, and continuous-space reasoning. By early November the research shifted to reliability, covering refusal, perception robustness, hallucination and unlearning.
editorial.whats_new: ROSE (Nov 6) proposes risk-aware orthogonal subspace navigation for lifelong knowledge editing in multimodal LLMs, targeting locality erosion and catastrophic forgetting.
editorial.why_it_matters: Multimodal models are being pushed toward deployable behavior: knowing when to refuse, resisting perceptual perturbation, avoiding hallucination, and being updated or unlearned after release.
editorial.take_for_builders: If you serve multimodal models, add evals for insufficient-evidence refusal and perceptual perturbation before adopting any of these techniques; treat them as preprints until independently reproduced.

status.detail: A cluster of arXiv papers moving from adding reasoning to multimodal models toward making them reliable and maintainable; all items are preprints.

storylines.label: Evaluating Tasks
storylines.latest_title: One Run Is Not Enough: A Monte Carlo Protocol for Evaluating LLM Reliability on Data Science Tasks

editorial.tldr: Late-October arXiv papers framed long-horizon agent work as an evaluation problem, with benchmarks for continual learning and web search alongside new critic, memory and multi-agent methods. On Nov 1 a paper questioned whether long-horizon terminal benchmarks actually measure depth.
editorial.whats_new: A Nov 6 paper argues one run is not enough and proposes a Monte Carlo protocol for measuring LLM reliability on data science tasks, following new consumer-task (LifeVal) and multilingual tool-use (τ-bench-LILT) benchmarks.
editorial.why_it_matters: Agent benchmark scores are only as trustworthy as the task design and run count behind them: depth, language coverage and run-to-run variance all change what a number means for your deployment.
editorial.take_for_builders: Rerun your internal agent evals several times and report the spread rather than a single score, and add non-English tool-use cases before trusting an English-only benchmark result.

status.detail: Research is shifting from adding long-horizon benchmarks to questioning their depth, language coverage and single-run reliability.

storylines.label: Benchmarking Memory
storylines.latest_title: MemoryDojo: Benchmarking Poisoning Through LLM Agent Memory

editorial.tldr: In October a paper benchmarked personal agent memory on interaction preferences, asking whether agents stop re-asking what users already told them. In early November, two more benchmarks moved the question from convenience to correctness and security.
editorial.whats_new: MemoryDojo (Nov 6) is a benchmark for poisoning attacks through LLM agent memory, where malicious instructions seen in one session can carry into later ones.
editorial.why_it_matters: Agent memory is now being evaluated for three distinct failure modes (burdensome re-asking, hallucinated memory, poisoning), so a memory layer needs tests for each, not just recall.
editorial.take_for_builders: If your agent persists memory across sessions, add a test that plants an instruction in one session and checks it is not acted on in the next, and treat stored memory as untrusted input.

status.detail: Three arXiv benchmarks in about two weeks each probe a different way agent memory can fail.
